title: Registering and Describing Tools
description: Define tools with clear names, descriptions, typed inputs, and examples so AI clients can call them correctly.

blocks.text: Tool registration is where backend logic becomes AI-callable. A well-described tool is easier for the model to select and easier for the client to validate. Bad descriptions are a leading cause of failed or misused tool calls.

blocks.title: What to include in each tool description
items: **Behavior** — what the tool does and when it should be used.
**Parameters** — names, types, required fields, and allowed values.
**Return shape** — what the tool returns on success and error.
**Examples** — one or two example invocations with expected results.
**Side effects** — whether the tool mutates data, sends emails, or triggers external systems.

blocks.title: Well-described tool in C#
blocks.content: A tool with rich metadata and validation.

blocks.title: Validation is non-negotiable
blocks.text: Validate inputs before executing business logic. Reject missing or invalid parameters with structured errors so the client can correct course.

items.text: My tool description explains when to use the tool
items.hint: Include behavior, parameters, return shape, examples, and side effects

items.text: I validate inputs before executing the tool
items.hint: Use schema validation or manual checks before business logic runs

items.text: My tool returns structured success and error results
items.hint: Separate success payloads from error messages with codes where useful

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Tool descriptions are part of the public API for AI clients.
Rich descriptions, typed schemas, and examples improve tool selection and execution.
Validation and structured errors make failures recoverable.
blocks.takeaway: Treat tool metadata as seriously as REST documentation. The model and client depend on it to use your backend correctly.
